newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.

text.p: The South African rand ended a roller-coaster day near its best levels, advancing nearly five cents against the dollar on the back of exporter demand for the currency.

The Reserve Bank was also active in the market after the rand softened initially, but a spokesman said its actions were small-scale and dealers agreed it was not primarily responsible for the day's sharp advance.

The stronger rand and steadier U.S. Treasuries helped bonds regain most of the ground lost on Tuesday, despite a sharp rise in the daily money market shortage to the highest level since April, at 10.608 billion rand.

"The SARB (central bank) definitely played a role but I don't think they were responsible for what happened. In the end I think it was more linked to one particular exporter," said UAL head of Treasury Peter Lane.
Lane said the market was going through a crunch period with liquidity extremely tight, but there could be light at the end of the tunnel.
"I think the markets may be anticipating a slightly more bullish situation early next year...although we've been disappointed a lot of times in the past."

The rand had started weaker, touching a morning low of 4.7290/7340 against the dollar, but the situation turned round soon after midday following significant exporter dollar sales, notably from one mining house, dealers said.
That also caught some domestic banks long of dollars, prompting further supply of the U.S. currency into the market.
A Reserve Bank spokesman told Reuters the central bank had been in the market but said the action was not aggressive.
"The Reserve Bank has not been aggressive. We were in the market but it was very, very small. I think what we are seeing is exporter-driven proceeds coming through," he said.
The rand was trading at 4.6730/6780 against the dollar at the 1400GMT local close but had pushed on to 4.6700/6750 by 1415GMT, from 4.7180/7230 on Tuesday.
With the rand safely back below 4.70, dealers said it now seemed unlikely the currency would re-test its October 31 record low of 4.7670 bid over the Christmas period, as many had feared last week.
Against the crosses, it was last at 7.8106/8320 against sterling from 7.9043/9174 and at 0.3317/3325 marks from 0.3270/3275.
The stronger currency helped long bonds with yields down eight basis points from Tuesday despite the grim money market shortage figures.
Traders said steadier U.S. Treasuries had helped and there was also patchy interest from local institutions, although turnover was low with many players already on holiday.
The market would be watching November CPI, due on Thursday at 0900 GMT, but with a poor number largely discounted it would take a major surprise to move bonds significantly.
"I don't think anybody is going to try and push it on the (CPI) figure unless it is particularly good or bad," said one bond trader.

A Reuters poll of nine economists forecast CPI would rise 9.5 percent year-on-year -- its highest level since July 1995 -- or 0.9 percent month-on-month, after a worse-than-expected 9.1 percent and 1.0 increase in October. Rising food prices are once again seen responsible.
The benchmark R150 was yielding 16.195 percent from 16.275 on Tuesday.
Bond Exchange statistics showed foreigners sold a net 55.32 million rand's worth of South African bonds on Tuesday after buying 192.52 million on Friday.
Nominal cumulative turnover was 2.21 billion rand on Tuesday from Friday's 3.27 billion rand.

Major banks quoted three-month NCD rates unchanged at between 17.40 and 17.75 percent while the 90-day BA rate was also steady at 16.70 to 17.00 percent, despite the jump in the money market shortage.
A Reserve Bank spokesman said the shortage of 10.608 billion rand on Tuesday, up from Saturday's 9.499 billion rand, was the highest since April 30, when it stood at 10.955 billion.
Monday was a public holiday in South Africa.
-- Ben Hirschler, Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
